# Tight midpoint comparisons: strict depth and a compact gap
Its dependencies are the newly proved finite midpoint-label center
theorem and the one-sided centroid-graph strictness lemma. Sections1--4
independently PASS in
`unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`.
The centroid-defect refinement also independently PASSes in Section7
of that audit.

Let P=conv(P) intersect Z^n be finite nonempty. Let d>=1 and let
K_p be positive d-dimensional compact convex bodies forming an actual
family: every anchored convex combination sum lambda_p p=q in P
obeys sum lambda_p K_p subset K_q. Write

    w_p=|K_p|, r_p=w_p^(1/d), M=sum_p w_p,
    k=number of occupied base parities, Gamma=(d/(d+1))^d.

Only these full-dimensional positive fibers are measured. The theorem
does not discard positive intrinsic boundary mass or claim an extension
to nonparallel lower-dimensional fibers.

## 1. A general centroid-graph sufficient condition

Suppose g_p is the ordinary centroid of K_p, and for EVERY distinct
same-parity pair p,q, with m=(p+q)/2, one has

    g_m=(g_p+g_q)/2.                                  (1)

Then maximum normalized mixed depth is at least Gamma/k. If |P|>k,
it is STRICTLY greater than Gamma/k.

Indeed T={(p,g_p):p in P}, with labels given by base parity, is closed
under geometric midpoints of equally labeled points. Give it weights
w_p. Section7 of
`candidate 58dcf29bfb78a573`
supplies an atomic full-ambient center y in T at level alpha=M/k.
If |P|>k, it supplies such a center whose minimal face in conv(T)
has weight strictly greater than alpha. Section6 of
`candidate fc860651e80d6fd0` transfers this
to respectively a weak or strict Gamma alpha bound for all closed
ambient halfspaces of the actual fiber measure. The selected point
is exactly one of the actual fiber centroids, so belongs to S.

For completeness, the weak transfer uses only the following direct
observation. Each fiber whose centroid belongs to a containing ambient
halfspace contributes at least Gamma of its volume by ordinary
Grunbaum, or its full volume if the restricted halfspace is constant.
The strict transfer additionally handles infimizing sequences with
unbounded integer tilts, as proved in that source. It is not obtained
by merely declaring each individual cap inequality strict.

The same weak bound holds when |P|=k and the labeled-point theorem
is in its exceptional case. No claim that (1) holds for arbitrary
actual fibers is being made.

## 2. Full tightness of midpoint BM implies the graph condition

Suppose, for EVERY distinct same-parity p,q and m=(p+q)/2,

    r_m=(r_p+r_q)/2.                                  (2)

Then (1) holds, so the conclusions of Section1 apply.

Convexity and ordinary Brunn--Minkowski give

    (K_p+K_q)/2 subset K_m,
    |K_m|^(1/d)>=|(K_p+K_q)/2|^(1/d)>=(r_p+r_q)/2.

Condition (2) makes both inequalities equalities. Positive compact
convex bodies with a proper inclusion in the same affine space have
strictly different volumes: separate an excluded point and mix it
with an interior ball to exhibit a positive ball in the difference.
Thus K_m=(K_p+K_q)/2. For d>=2 the equality case of ordinary BM says
K_p and K_q are positively homothetic; for d=1 every positive interval
is homothetic to every other. Write K_p=aK+t and K_q=bK+s with a,b>0.
The Minkowski midpoint is ((a+b)/2)K+(t+s)/2, whose centroid is exactly
(g_p+g_q)/2. This proves (1), without asserting general additivity of
centroids under Minkowski sums.

Requiring (2) only on a chosen tree or forest is insufficient. The
proof explicitly needs all pairs in each parity class; the archived
zero-forest counterexample does not meet this hypothesis.

## 3. A uniform separation from midpoint tightness on a fixed compact class

Fix P,d, R>0, and v>0, and assume |P|>k. Consider all actual families
satisfying

    K_p subset R B_d,       |K_p|>=v for every p in P.

Define the nonnegative scalar midpoint deficit

    E(K)=max_{p!=q, p congruent q mod2}
          [ |K_((p+q)/2)|^(1/d)
                    -( |K_p|^(1/d)+|K_q|^(1/d) )/2 ]. (3)

The pair list is nonempty by |P|>k. There exists epsilon>0, depending
on these fixed data, such that

    E(K)<=epsilon  implies  maximum depth>Gamma/k.    (4)

Equivalently every family in this normalized compact class with depth
at most Gamma/k has E(K)>epsilon. This is a compact positive gap, not
an explicit dimension-only modulus and not a saturation theorem for
local minima.

Here are the full compactness and continuity details. The space of
nonempty compact convex subsets of R B_d is compact in Hausdorff
distance. Taking the finite product and imposing the closed conditions
|K_p|>=v and all anchored inclusions leaves a compact space X. Volumes
are continuous under bounded convex Hausdorff convergence. Anchored
inclusions are closed by approximating each chosen source point and
keeping its convex coefficients fixed. There are finitely many fibers;
all limits have positive volume by the bound v.

The maximum normalized mixed depth D(K) is continuous on X. Fiber
indicators converge in L1, so the raw mixed measures converge in total
variation. At a fixed candidate this uniformly controls every cap
mass. Moving a candidate by t in one fixed base fiber changes each
nonvertical cap threshold by at most t after normalizing its continuous
normal. Each fiber lies in R B_d, so the slab has volume at most
kappa_(d-1)R^(d-1)t, including d=1 with kappa_0=1. Sum over |P|
fibers. Vertical caps do not change under this movement. Approximating
a limit maximizer in its fixed fiber proves the lower-limit inequality;
taking maximizing candidates and a subsequence with fixed base and
convergent continuous coordinate proves the upper-limit inequality.
Hausdorff convergence ensures the limit belongs to the corresponding
fiber. Total masses converge and stay at least |P|v, giving continuity
after normalization. The same estimates show each family's maximum
is attained on its finite union of compact candidate fibers.

Formula (3) is the maximum of finitely many continuous functions, so
is continuous. The bad subset X_bad={K in X:D(K)<=Gamma/k} is compact.
If it is empty, any positive epsilon gives (4). Otherwise E attains a
minimum e on it. Nonnegativity follows from BM. If e=0, (2) holds
for every relevant pair at an attained bad family, while Section2
gives D(K)>Gamma/k, a contradiction. Hence e>0. Choosing epsilon=e/2
proves (4).

This argument proves the existence and positivity of the constant;
neither is an unproved compactness assertion. It does not keep the
constant uniform when the base changes, volumes vanish, or bounding
normalizations degenerate.

## 4. Relation to the unresolved attained-minimum route

The audited arithmetic attainment reduction gives |P|>k, a fixed
lattice-complete base, and positive normalized compact families for
any hypothetical strict bad minimum. This note therefore supplies a
new necessary feature of such a family: at least one same-parity
midpoint comparison has a definite positive BM root deficit in its
fixed normalization. It does NOT show that a feasible deformation can
reduce that deficit while decreasing maximum normalized depth.

The normal-preserving transport, parity triangulation, and near-parity
expansion results remain separate. Their known obstructions prevent
silently identifying boundary transport energy with (3), or adding
overlapping midpoint contributions. The all-direction numerical
inequality for arbitrary positive midpoint deficit is still missing.

## 5. A stronger necessary centroid-defect gap

In the same fixed compact class X of Section3 define

    E_cent(K)=max_{p!=q, p congruent q mod2}
                |g_((p+q)/2)-(g_p+g_q)/2|.            (5)

If X_bad is nonempty, E_cent has a strictly positive minimum on it.
Consequently sufficiently small E_cent also implies a strict
Gamma/k bound, with a constant depending only on the fixed compact
class data. This statement is stronger than requiring a positive
BM root deficit somewhere: a BM shape gap may coexist with exact
centroid midpoint identities and hence with the strict safe regime.

Proof: centroid coordinates are continuous under the bounded convex
Hausdorff limits in X. Their numerator integrals converge by bounded
L1 convergence, and their denominators stay at least v. Thus (5) is
continuous. It attains a minimum on compact X_bad. A zero minimum
would give (1) at an attained bad family, contradicting the STRICT
conclusion of Section1 since |P|>k. Hence the minimum is positive.
Half that minimum gives the asserted neighborhood, exactly as in
Section3. If X_bad is empty the implication is vacuous.

This is a necessary obstruction at a hypothetical bad minimum, not
a deformation decreasing it. In particular a nonzero scalar BM root
gap need not mean that a target strictly contains its endpoint
Minkowski midpoint. Orthogonally elongated rectangles can have a
positive BM gap even when the target IS exactly that Minkowski
midpoint and its centroid midpoint defect vanishes.
